statement: In people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl and who had taken buprenorphine after fentanyl, remembering severe withdrawal on taking it was common, and more common the shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, in one self-report survey analysed without adjustment (Varshneya et al., 2022, read from the author manuscript). Of 1,679 people whose answers were collected at admission by an outcomes-tracking system, 1,163 (69.3%) reported fentanyl use; 421 of them had never taken buprenorphine after fentanyl and 57 had done so only with a shortest wait of 1 month to 1 year. Of the 685 whose shortest wait was under 1 month, 250 (36.5%; 95% CI 33.0 to 40.2, editors' calculation) said their withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine after fentanyl had been severe, 136 (19.9%) moderate, 122 (17.8%) mild and 177 (25.8%) none; of 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl, 30 (15.0%) said severe. Severe withdrawal after buprenorphine was remembered by 152 of the 339 people whose shortest wait was under 24 hours (44.8%) and 55 of the 160 whose shortest wait was 24 to 48 hours (34.4%), and, by the editors' reconstruction from the printed odds ratios (checked against the bars of Figure 1), by 25 of 97 at 48 to 72 hours (25.8%), 13 of 52 at 72 hours to 1 week (25.0%) and 5 of 37 at 1 week to 1 month (13.5%): a gradual fall, with no clear cut-off. The abstract's 22.19% for 'those who waited less than 24 hours' is 152 out of all 685, not out of the 339 who waited less than 24 hours (editors' calculation). The paper's odds ratios for severe withdrawal (under 24 hours 5.20, 95% CI 1.98 to 13.68; 24 to 48 hours 3.35, 1.24 to 9.09; 48 to 72 hours 2.22, 0.78 to 6.33; 72 hours to 1 week 2.13, 0.69 to 6.62) are unadjusted and compare each group with a reference the paper does not name, which the editors' exact reproduction shows to be the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month; the results call the odds ratios of about 2 at 48 hours to 1 week no increase, and the conclusion compares with everyone who waited more than 48 hours, which the model did not do. The answers were remembered when people entered treatment, about one or more unspecified occasions; the shortest wait ever was not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal; the survey did not record the dose, form, setting or supervision of the buprenorphine, or whether withdrawal had begun before it was taken; and a single rating cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it did not relieve (the authors explain severe withdrawal after methadone as too little opioid effect early in treatment). The survey period, response rate, full questionnaire and centres are not described, and the descriptive appendix was not on file. Among the 152 people who had taken both medicines after fentanyl, 69 (45.4%) remembered severe withdrawal after buprenorphine and 20 (13.2%) after methadone. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Can Suboxone put you in withdrawal if you use fentanyl? Many people say it did. In a survey of people starting treatment at 49 US centres who said they used fentanyl, 250 of 685 who had taken buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal when they took it, 37 in 100, against 15 in 100 of those who had taken methadone after fentanyl. The shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, the more often they remembered severe withdrawal: about 45 in 100 when it was under a day, 34 in 100 at one to two days, about 25 in 100 at two days to a week and 14 in 100 at a week to a month, with no clear cut-off. These are memories collected when people started treatment, about occasions nobody recorded. The survey did not know the dose, the form or who gave it, it allowed for nothing else that differed between people, and one question cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it failed to relieve. The paper's own summary gives 22 in 100 for those who waited under a day, but that is out of all 685 people, not out of the 339 who waited that little.
population: People entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres using one outcomes-tracking system (survey period and centres not described) whose main drug was opioids and who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl before treatment: 1,163 of 1,679 (mean age 30.8 years; 70.6% men; 80.4% White; 43.9% said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission); withdrawal ratings analysed for the 685 whose shortest wait after fentanyl before buprenorphine was under 1 month and for 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl
exposure: Taking buprenorphine after fentanyl (any product; the table note names seven brands, Suboxone among them), grouped by the shortest time people said they had ever waited after fentanyl: under 24 hours, 24 to 48 hours, 48 to 72 hours, 72 hours to 1 week, 1 week to 1 month; dose, form, setting and supervision not recorded
comparator: Shorter against longer shortest waits (reference, by the editors' reproduction of the printed odds ratios: the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month); methadone taken after fentanyl (200 people; 199 in the odds model); no adjustment for anything
outcome: Self-rated withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine (or methadone) after fentanyl, remembered at treatment entry (none, mild, moderate or severe; one item, not a validated scale); the authors take severe withdrawal after buprenorphine as precipitated withdrawal
magnitude: Varshneya et al. (2022), Table 1 and text. Fentanyl use reported by 1,163 of 1,679 (69.3%; probably 180, definitely 983). Shortest wait before buprenorphine (of 1,163): under 24 h 339 (29.1%), 24–48 h 160 (13.8%), 48–72 h 97 (8.3%), 72 h–1 week 52 (4.5%), 1 week–1 month 37 (3.2%), 1 month–1 year 57 (4.9%), never 421 (36.2%); methadone 135, 22, 21, 13, 8, 29 and 935. Withdrawal after buprenorphine (N = 685): severe 250 (36.5%; Wilson 95% CI 33.0–40.2, editors), moderate 136 (19.9%), mild 122 (17.8%), none 177 (25.8%); after methadone (N = 200): severe 30 (15.0%; 10.7–20.6), moderate 29 (14.5%), mild 44 (22.0%), none 97 (48.5%). Severe within each waiting group (editors' calculation; the last three counts reconstructed from the printed odds ratios, adding up to 250 and matching Figure 1): 152/339 = 44.8% (Wilson 39.6–50.2), 55/160 = 34.4% (27.5–42.0), 25/97 = 25.8% (18.1–35.3), 13/52 = 25.0% (15.2–38.2), 5/37 = 13.5% (5.9–28.0); methadone 23/135 = 17.0%, 2/22, 2/21, 1/13 and 2/8. As printed in the abstract and results: 22.19% (152/685) and 8.03% (55/685); methadone 11.56% (23/199) and 1.01% (2/199). Odds ratios for severe withdrawal, unadjusted, against the 1 week–1 month group (editors' reproduction): buprenorphine 5.202 (95% CI 1.979–13.675; p = 0.001), 3.352 (1.237–9.089; p = 0.017), 2.222 (0.780–6.329; p = 0.135), 2.133 (0.687–6.620; p = 0.190); methadone 0.616 (0.117–3.247), 0.300 (0.035–2.606), 0.316 (0.036–2.750), 0.250 (0.019–3.342). Both medicines (n = 152): severe after buprenorphine 69 (45.4%), after methadone 20 (13.2%). 483 of 1,163 (41.5%) knew someone who used fentanyl and had precipitated withdrawal after buprenorphine. Complete relief of withdrawal: 68 of 177 (38.4%) for buprenorphine and 43 of 97 (44.3%) for methadone, denominators equal to the numbers reporting no withdrawal symptoms (who was asked is not stated).

evidence.locator: Abstract, Methods (p. 1); Methods › Sample and Assessments; Methods › Statistical Analyses (p. 2)
evidence.extracted: Self-report data from 1,679 people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment facilities, collected by a third-party aggregation system (Trac9) to track treatment outcomes at routine admission and received de-identified. People whose primary drug was opioids and who reported probably or definitely using fentanyl were asked whether they had used buprenorphine (or methadone, as a comparator) after fentanyl, the time between the two, and whether the medicine relieved or worsened their withdrawal. Severe withdrawal was analysed by binary logistic regression; descriptive statistics are in Appendix 1 (not on file). No survey period, centre description or response rate is given.

evidence.extracted: The authors suggest that fentanyl, which accumulates in fat with repeated use and can take weeks to clear, can be displaced by buprenorphine, and that this may contribute to withdrawal within 48 hours of fentanyl use even with conventional starting procedures; they hypothesize that severe withdrawal after methadone may reflect poorly managed withdrawal from too little opioid effect early in treatment, because first outpatient doses are capped and methadone takes more than a week to reach steady levels. The Conclusions say that people who take buprenorphine within 24 to 48 hours of fentanyl are at significantly greater risk of severe withdrawal than those who wait more than 48 hours, a comparison the model did not make (the paper names no reference group; by the editors' reconstruction it was the 1 week-1 month group).

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_varshneya_2022 (JBI prevalence checklist; editors' summary high): answers remembered at treatment entry about unspecified occasions, one unvalidated self-rating, sample frame, period and response rate not described, the shortest wait ever not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal, no adjustment, and headline percentages with the wrong denominators.

inconsistency.note: One survey; no conflicting data were read.

indirectness.note: The outcome measured (severe withdrawal remembered on taking buprenorphine after fentanyl) is not the same as withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine, which a single rating cannot separate from withdrawal it did not relieve; dose, form and setting are unknown, so nothing transfers to supervised starts.

imprecision.note: The overall share is precise (33.0% to 40.2%), but the gradient is measured against a reference group of 37 people with 5 severe ratings (odds ratio under 24 hours 1.98 to 13.68; the ratios at 48 hours to 1 week include 1).

grade.reasoning: A cross-sectional self-report survey starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). Rated as worded: how often people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine following fentanyl, and its association with the shortest wait they reported. It cannot give the incidence of withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine, or show that waiting longer prevents it, and no gradient was used to upgrade (unadjusted, self-reported groups). Status: single study; the paper cites only case reports and anecdotal accounts as earlier evidence. The waiting times appear only as the survey's groups, never as advice.
